The **Class A premium over 1970s Class C** is about **$500/month (about 20%)**. 1970s product has the highest occupancy (97.1%) because it is the cheapest option.

### By city (practical spreads)
Broker reports don't split class by city publicly. Use the city ranking (Q41) plus the vintage spread:
- **Thousand Oaks / Newbury Park / Oak Park:** strongest Class A (Sanctuary, Hillcrest-area projects). Expect about $3,000-3,400 for a new 2BR vs. the mid-$2,000s for 1970s garden units.
- **Camarillo:** new product (Calixa, AMLI Camarillo, Anacapa Canyon) is close to Thousand Oaks pricing, with a big gap to 1970s stock near Old Town.
- **Oxnard:** Riverpark product (Panorama, Tempo) lists 1BRs around **$2,675** (Redfin search snapshot). Older south Oxnard and La Colonia stock rents several hundred dollars less and has the highest overcrowding (Q58).
- **Ventura:** 2010s product (The Willows, Westview-area projects) vs. Midtown and Westside 1950s-70s buildings. Ventura has the county's largest pre-1960 share.
- **Simi Valley / Moorpark:** younger stock overall, so the spread is narrower.

### In-place vs. market
ACS in-place median gross rent (2020-24) is $2,249 for a 2BR countywide and $1,940 in Oxnard. That includes utilities and long tenancies, so older Class C buildings often run **20-30% below** the Class A asking rent.

**So what:** The upside in a Class C deal is closing part of the roughly $500 gap through renovation plus turnover. It is not reaching Class A rents.

### Where concessions are showing up (fall 2026)
- **Oxnard, Riverpark / north Oxnard:** Redfin search results for Riverpark studios carry a **"2 MONTHS FREE"** tag, and Del Norte-area 1BRs show **"6 WEEKS FREE."** This is the zone with Panorama (333 units, opened Q3 2025), Tempo Riverpark and Town Square at Wagon Wheel.
- **Camarillo:** Calixa (385 units) delivered in Q1 2026, and CoStar vacancy sits at 7.4%. Expect lease-up specials of about 4-8 weeks.

- **Thousand Oaks / Newbury Park:** watch the Sanctuary (218 units) as it leases in 2026-27.
- Matthews' H1 2026 report notes Class A operators are "leaning on" concessions to hold face rents. CBRE's flat rents (+0.1% QoQ) point the same way.

### How big
| Offer | Effective discount on a 12-month lease |
|---|---|
| 2 weeks free | about 4% |
| 4 weeks / 1 month free | about 8% |
| 6 weeks free | about 12% |
| 2 months free | about 17% |

Lease-up concessions usually come with look-and-lease deadlines, waived fees or parking. Stabilized Class A typically offers 0-4 weeks. Class B/C mostly uses a lower deposit or a prorated first month.

### Underwriting implications
- **Use effective rent, not face rent,** for new-product comps. A $2,700 face 1BR with 6 weeks free nets about $2,380.
- Renewal risk rises for Class B owners within about 1 mile of a lease-up. Budget for slower renewal increases, not cuts in asking rent.
- Concessions should fade during 2027 because the pipeline dropped to about 1.3% of stock and Q2 2026 had zero deliveries.

answers.summary: On long-held buildings, in-place rents commonly sit 15-30% below market. Under AB 1482 you can raise rents at most 8.6% between Aug 2026 and Jul 2027 (5% + 3.6% California CPI), so closing a 20% gap takes about 2-3 years of maximum increases, plus resets to market when units turn over. In Oxnard and Ojai, local 4% caps on older buildings stretch that to about 5 years.
answers.answer:
### How big is loss-to-lease?
- **Market:** CBRE Q2 2026 2BR $2,914; CoStar 2BR asking $2,713.
- **In-place proxy:** ACS 2024 median gross rent for a 2BR is **$2,292**, and that includes tenant-paid utilities. Contract rent on long-tenure units is lower still.
- **Practical range:** Mom-and-pop buildings held 10-20+ years often show **15-30% loss-to-lease**, and individual 10-year+ tenants sometimes 35%+. Professionally managed assets are usually 3-8%.

### The law (statewide; check local ordinances)
- **AB 1482 / Civil Code 1947.12:** annual increases capped at **5% plus regional CPI, maximum 10%**, measured from the lowest rent in the prior 12 months. Ventura County is not one of the 10 counties with a regional BLS index, so it uses the **California CPI**, which rose 3.6% April to April. That makes the cap **8.6%** for increases taking effect **Aug 1, 2026 through Jul 31, 2027** (see Q117).
- **Local caps:** Oxnard limits increases to **4%** a year on buildings first occupied before Feb 1, 1995, and Ojai has a 4% cap as well (see Q133).
- **Exempt:** buildings less than 15 years old (rolling), single-family homes and condos owned by individuals with the required notice, and owner-occupied duplexes.
- **Vacancy decontrol:** rent resets to market on voluntary vacancy (Costa-Hawkins).
- **Just cause (Civil Code 1946.2):** after 12 months of tenancy, no-fault terminations (substantial remodel, owner move-in, withdrawal from the market) require one month's rent in relocation. "Substantial remodel" is narrowly defined and requires permits and a vacancy of at least 30 days.
- **Notice:** 30 days for increases of 10% or less; 90 days for more than 10% (Civil Code 827).

### Capture math
A 20% gap closes in about **2.2 years** at 8.6% a year (1.086^2 = 1.18, 1.086^3 = 1.28). Under a 4% local cap (Oxnard, Ojai) it takes about **4.6 years** (1.04^5 = 1.22). Add natural turnover: about 13% of renters move each year (Q52), and those units reset to market.

**Underwriting:** Model rent bumps at the AB 1482 cap only where you can document market support. Assume about 10-15% annual turnover to market, and don't count on remodel evictions.

Typical loss-to-lease on long-held mom-and-pop buildings: 15-30%
Oxnard and Ojai cap older buildings at 4% a year, which roughly doubles the time to close a gap
A 20% gap takes about 2-3 years of maximum increases

answers.summary: Plan for roughly $6,500-$9,000 per unit per year (about 35-45% of income) on an older small building after a sale reassesses the property tax, and about $9,500-$13,000 per unit on a newer large community, where higher assessed values, payroll and amenities push costs up.
answers.answer:
### Working ranges (annual, per unit, Ventura County, 2026 dollars)
| Line item | Older small (5-30 units, 1960s-80s) | Newer large (150+ units, 2000+) |
|---|---|---|
| Property tax, reassessed at purchase (~1.1-1.2% of price plus direct assessments) | $3,300-$4,200 (at $280-350K/unit) | $5,200-$6,000 (at $450-520K/unit) |
| Insurance | $900-$1,800 | $800-$1,400 |
| Water / sewer / trash, if owner-paid | $1,300-$1,800 | $700-$1,300 (often billed back) |
| Common-area electric / gas | $200-$500 | $400-$700 |
| Repairs, maintenance and turnover | $900-$1,500 | $900-$1,300 |
| Payroll (on-site staff) | $0-$300 | $1,600-$2,500 |
| Management fee | 4-6% of income ($1,200-$1,700) | 2.5-3.5% ($900-$1,200) |
| Admin, marketing, landscaping, contracts | $300-$600 | $700-$1,200 |
| **Total before reserves** | **about $6,500-$9,000** | **about $9,500-$13,000** |
| Replacement reserves | $350-$600 | $250-$350 |

### Local anchors
- **Utilities:** Ventura Housing's June 2025 utility allowance for a multifamily 2BR is $50 water + $50 sewer + $36 trash, or about **$136/month ($1,630/year)**. That is a good proxy for owner-paid water, sewer and trash in the City of Ventura.
- **Property tax:** California's Prop 13 base rate is 1% plus voter-approved debt and direct assessments (Mello-Roos, lighting, school bonds). Effective rates are about 1.05-1.25% depending on tax rate area. Don't use the seller's tax bill.
- **Insurance** is the most volatile line (Q48).

### Rules of thumb
- Expense ratio: 35-45% for older small buildings, 30-38% for newer large ones. Lenders usually underwrite at least 35% and require at least $250-300/unit in reserves.
- Older buildings save on payroll but spend more on plumbing, roofs and deferred maintenance.

answers.summary: Habitational property insurance in coastal Southern California roughly doubled over 2023-2026 for many owners. Older wood-frame buildings and anything near brush saw the biggest jumps. Admitted carriers pulled back, so more apartment owners now rely on surplus-lines (E&S) markets or the California FAIR Plan plus a wrap-around (DIC) policy.
answers.answer:
### What happened
- **Carrier pullback:** In 2022-2024 several large admitted insurers paused or restricted new California property business. State Farm General stopped taking new property applications in 2023 and later non-renewed tens of thousands of policies, including commercial apartment policies. Allstate also paused. Remaining admitted carriers tightened underwriting on older construction, fire zones and loss history.
- **State response:** The Department of Insurance's **Sustainable Insurance Strategy** (announced Sept 2023, key regulations finalized Dec 2024) lets insurers use forward-looking catastrophe models and pass through California reinsurance costs. In exchange, insurers commit to write in wildfire-distressed areas (at least 85% of their statewide market share). Expect rate increases to continue, with somewhat better availability from 2026 on.
- **FAIR Plan:** Covers commercial habitational buildings, including individually owned buildings with **5 or more units**. It is a **named-peril** policy (fire, lightning, internal explosion; vandalism optional), so owners add a difference-in-conditions (DIC) policy for liability, water damage and other perils.

### Magnitude (practitioner range)
- Many Ventura County apartment owners saw **premium increases of 30-100%+ over three years**. Deductibles and wildfire sublimits rose, and coverage often moved from replacement cost to stated limits.
- Exposure is greatest in Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zones (Ventura hillsides, Ojai, Camarillo Heights after the 2024 Mountain Fire, Simi Valley and Thousand Oaks edges, Oak Park) and for pre-1980 frame buildings with older wiring or plumbing.
- Flat coastal Oxnard, Port Hueneme and central Ventura usually price better but carry flood and tsunami questions.

### Who still writes
A mix of admitted commercial carriers (selectively), E&S markets through wholesale brokers, apartment-association group programs, and the FAIR Plan plus DIC as a last resort.

**So what:** Get a binding quote before removing contingencies. Underwrite insurance at **$900-$1,800 per unit** for older buildings, and stress-test DSCR for another 20-30% increase at renewal.

answers.summary: Water in Ventura County is fragmented: city utilities (Ventura, Oxnard, Camarillo, Thousand Oaks, Santa Paula, Fillmore, Port Hueneme), county waterworks districts (Moorpark, much of Simi Valley), investor-owned utilities (Cal Am, Golden State) and special districts (Casitas, Camrosa, Triunfo). Owner-paid water, sewer and trash typically runs about $110-$160 per unit per month.

### Who serves where (retail water / sewer)
| Area | Water | Sewer |
|---|---|---|
| Ventura | City of Ventura (Ventura Water); Casitas MWD and groundwater supply | Ventura Water |
| Oxnard | City of Oxnard (Calleguas MWD imported water, United WCD and local groundwater, recycled water) | City of Oxnard |
| Port Hueneme | City / Port Hueneme Water Agency (with Oxnard) | City of Port Hueneme |
| Camarillo | City of Camarillo; Camrosa Water District (east/south Camarillo, CSUCI, Santa Rosa Valley) | Camarillo Sanitary District / Camrosa |
| Thousand Oaks / Newbury Park | City of Thousand Oaks and California American Water (split service areas); Calleguas wholesale | City of Thousand Oaks |
| Simi Valley | Ventura County Waterworks District No. 8 and Golden State Water | City of Simi Valley |
| Moorpark | Ventura County Waterworks District No. 1 | VCWWD No. 1 |
| Oak Park | Triunfo Water & Sanitation District | Triunfo |
| Ojai | Casitas MWD (took over the former Golden State system) | Ojai Valley Sanitary District |
| Santa Paula / Fillmore | City-owned groundwater systems | City |

**Wholesalers:** Calleguas MWD (State Water Project via Metropolitan) serves East County, Camarillo and Oxnard. Casitas MWD (Lake Casitas) serves the Ventura River and Ojai side. United Water Conservation District manages Santa Clara River groundwater recharge.

- Ventura Housing's June 2025 multifamily utility allowance (City of Ventura) per month: **water $40-62, sewer $40-59, trash $33-36**. That is about **$136 for a 2BR** and **$157 for a 3BR**.

- Trash is franchised by city (Oxnard runs its own), and SB 1383 organics rules added multifamily bin costs.

### So what
- Identify the retail purveyor **by parcel** before underwriting. Rates, drought surcharges and connection fees vary a lot even inside one city (Thousand Oaks, Camarillo).
- For value-add, separate water submeters or RUBS (Q50) can recover $75-150 per unit per month where leases allow.

answers.summary: RUBS (ratio utility billing) for water, sewer and trash is common in professionally managed Ventura County apartments and growing in value-add deals. It is legal if clearly disclosed in the lease, but you can't add it to an existing tenancy without consent. Gas and electric can't be resold above utility tariffs, and new buildings must submeter water.
answers.answer:
### How common
- **Class A and newer communities:** Standard. Water, sewer, trash and sometimes pest control are billed back by submeter or RUBS through a third-party billing company. Typical charges run about $75-150 per unit per month.
- **Older mom-and-pop buildings:** Usually all-inclusive rent with owner-paid water, sewer and trash. That is one of the main value-add levers after a sale.

### Legal framework (California; verify specifics with counsel)
1. **Water submetering law (Civil Code 1954.201 et seq., SB 7 of 2016).** New multiunit buildings permitted after Jan 1, 2018 must have water submeters. When a landlord bills submetered water, the law limits what can be charged (no profit on water, capped fees and late charges) and requires specific lease disclosures.
2. **RUBS (allocation without meters)** is not banned by state statute for water, sewer and trash. It must be clearly disclosed in the lease (allocation formula, billing company, estimated amounts), and billing must not exceed the owner's actual cost.
3. **Gas and electric** resale is governed by Public Utilities Code 739.5. Master-metered owners can't charge more than the utility's rate, so RUBS for electricity is generally avoided.
4. **Shared meters (Civil Code 1940.9):** If a tenant's meter serves areas outside their unit, the landlord must disclose it and agree on an allocation.
5. **Existing tenants:** Adding RUBS mid-tenancy changes lease terms. It can't be imposed unilaterally, and it may be treated as rent under AB 1482's cap. Most owners add RUBS **at turnover** or at the renewal of a fixed-term lease.

### Investor so-what
- On a building where the owner pays water, sewer and trash at about $136 per 2BR per month (Q49), RUBS on new leases can add **$1,200-$1,600 per unit per year** of NOI over 3-5 years as units turn. At a 5% cap rate that is about $24K-$32K of value per unit.
- Underwrite the ramp at your turnover rate (about 13-20% a year), not all at once.
- Check whether a city rent ordinance or HUD/LIHTC regulatory agreement restricts bill-backs.
keyPoints: New multiunit buildings permitted after Jan 1, 2018 must have water submeters (SB 7, Civil Code 1954.201+)
RUBS for water/sewer/trash is legal with clear lease disclosure and no markup
Gas/electric can't be resold above the utility tariff (PUC 739.5)
You can't add RUBS to an existing tenancy without consent; add it at turnover
Typical bill-back: about $75-150 per unit per month

answers.summary: Third-party management for small and mid-size Ventura County apartments usually costs 4-6% of collected income, often with a monthly minimum and a leasing fee. Institutional 150+ unit communities run about 2.5-3.5%. The market is split between national operators running Class A and a deep bench of local and regional firms running older stock.
answers.answer:
### Typical fee structures (2026 practitioner ranges)
| Property type | Base fee | Common add-ons |
|---|---|---|
| 2-4 units | 6-10% or $75-$125 per unit/month minimum | Leasing fee of 50-100% of one month; renewal fee $150-$300 |
| 5-50 units | 4-6% of collections | Leasing fee $300-$600 or 25-50% of a month; construction management 5-10% of project cost |
| 50-150 units | 3-4.5% plus on-site payroll | Lease-up fee; accounting/IT fees |
| 150+ unit Class A | 2.5-3.5% plus full on-site staff | Lease-up / marketing fees; asset management by owner |

Other common charges: a setup fee of about $250-$500 per property, eviction coordination, and markups on maintenance labor. Read the management agreement for termination terms (30-60 days is typical).

### Who manages
- **Institutional / REIT-managed Class A:** Large owners such as **Essex Property Trust** self-manage. Most of the 2015-2026 new-construction communities (Riverpark, Camarillo, Thousand Oaks) are run by national third-party operators or the developer's own management arm.
- **Affordable / public:** Ventura Housing, the Area Housing Authority, Many Mansions and other nonprofits manage their own portfolios. Tax credit deals often use specialist third-party managers.
- **Local and regional firms:** Most 5-50 unit buildings in Ventura, Oxnard, Camarillo and the Conejo Valley are run by local residential and commercial property managers, including firms that also manage HOAs, plus Santa Barbara-based firms extending south. California Oaks Property Management Company, for example, appears in Ventura Housing's landlord materials.
- **Self-management** is still common among long-held family owners, which is often where loss-to-lease and deferred maintenance are found.

### How to build the list
Use HUD/HCD and CTCAC compliance lists for affordable managers, the **NARPM** and **IREM** chapter directories, the "managed by" field on CoStar property records, and DRE broker license lookups (property managers need a broker license in California).

**So what:** A 5% fee vs. self-management is about $1,500 per unit per year of NOI on a $2,500 rent. Buyers will underwrite it even if the seller self-manages.
keyPoints: Small/mid buildings: 4-6% of collections; 2-4 units often 6-10% or a monthly minimum
Institutional 150+ units: about 2.5-3.5% plus on-site payroll
Leasing fees of 25-100% of one month's rent are common
California property managers must hold a DRE broker license (or work under one)
Buyers underwrite a management fee even when the seller self-manages

answers.summary: Ventura County renters stay put. Only about 13% of people in renter households moved in the past year, and about half of renter households moved in before 2020 (ACS 2024). Annual unit turnover is about 15-25% for older stabilized buildings and 35-45% for Class A, with Heritage Valley and Ojai renters staying longest.
answers.answer:
### Census data
**Move-in year, renter households (ACS 2024 1-year, county):**
| Moved in | Share |
|---|---|
| 2023 or later | 21.9% |
| 2020-2022 | 26.4% |
| 2010-2019 | 37.3% |
| 2000-2009 | 10.6% |
| Before 2000 | 3.7% |

About **52% of renter households have been in place since before 2020**, and about 14% since before 2010.

**Mobility:** In 2024, 86.9% of people living in renter households were in the same home as a year earlier. Implied annual mobility is about **13%** of renter-household residents, with most moves (about 23,000 of 36,000) staying within the county.

**By city (ACS 2020-24, share of renters who moved in before 2010):** Fillmore 34%, Ojai 32%, Oxnard 19%, Ventura 16%, Thousand Oaks 14%, Santa Paula 14%, Simi Valley 12%, Port Hueneme 12%, Camarillo 9%, Moorpark 9%. The Camarillo and Moorpark numbers reflect newer stock and more mobile tenants.

### What that means for operators
- **Turnover by property type (practitioner ranges):** 15-25% a year for older Class B/C with below-market rents, where tenants are "locked in" by loss-to-lease. 30-45% for Class A, with more movers and first-time renters. Military-heavy Port Hueneme (NBVC) and student-adjacent Camarillo (CSUCI) run higher.
- **Average tenure:** Roughly 3-5 years in Class A and 6-10+ years in older buildings, with some tenancies over 20 years.
- Low turnover is a **double-edged sword**. It means stable cash flow and low make-ready spending, but it slows capture of loss-to-lease under AB 1482 (Q46).

**So what:** In acquisition models for older stock, use 15-20% annual turnover. Using a 40% national-average turnover rate will overstate how fast you can mark rents to market.
keyPoints: ACS 2024: about 52% of county renter households moved in before 2020
About 13% of renter-household residents moved in the past year (86.9% same house)
Longest tenure: Fillmore and Ojai (about a third of renters moved in before 2010)
Practitioner turnover: 15-25%/yr older B/C vs 30-45%/yr Class A

answers.summary: Budget about $1,500-$3,000 for a light turn on a short-tenure unit, $5,000-$10,000 for a medium turn, and $15,000-$35,000+ when a 10-20 year tenant leaves a 1970s unit that needs flooring, kitchen and bath work. Add 30-60 days of lost rent for the bigger jobs.
answers.answer:
### Typical turn scopes (Ventura County, 2026 practitioner ranges)
| Scope | What's included | Cost per unit | Downtime |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Light turn** (1-3 year tenant) | Paint, clean, carpet clean or patch LVP, minor repairs, rekey, smoke/CO detectors | $1,500-$3,000 | 7-14 days |
| **Medium turn** | Full paint, new LVP flooring, blinds, light fixtures, some appliances, faucet/hardware | $5,000-$10,000 | 14-30 days |
| **Heavy / long-tenure turn** (10-20+ years) | Above plus cabinets/counters, bath refresh (tub reglaze or surround, vanity, toilet), electrical/plumbing fixes, possibly window or slider | $15,000-$35,000+ | 30-60 days |

### Local cost drivers
- **Labor:** Coastal Southern California rates. Licensed contractors needed for electrical and plumbing, with permits required for most kitchen and bath work in Ventura, Oxnard and Thousand Oaks.
- **Older buildings:** 1960s-70s units can have galvanized pipe, ungrounded wiring, asbestos (popcorn ceilings, flooring mastic) and lead paint. Testing and abatement can add $1,500-$5,000 or more to a heavy turn.
- **Habitability:** Units must meet Civil Code 1941.1 standards (hot water, heat, weatherproofing, pest-free) before re-renting. Code enforcement in older Oxnard and Ventura neighborhoods is active.
- **Smoke and CO detectors, water-conserving fixtures** (Civil Code 1101.4) and **balcony/deck inspections** (SB 721, for 3+ unit buildings with elevated elements) add one-time costs.

### Underwriting tips
- Budget make-ready as a per-turn cost multiplied by the expected turnover rate (Q52), not a flat per-unit figure.
- Example: an older building with 20% annual turnover and an average turn of $4,000 needs about **$800 per unit per year** in turnover costs. That sits inside the repairs-and-maintenance line (Q47).
- Units with long-tenure tenants should carry a separate **renovation budget** at turnover, because that is when the loss-to-lease is captured (Q54).
keyPoints: Light turn: about $1,500-$3,000; medium: about $5,000-$10,000
Long-tenure 1970s unit: $15,000-$35,000+ and 30-60 days down
Budget turnover cost = average turn cost x turnover rate (e.g., $4,000 x 20% = $800/unit/yr)
Older stock may need asbestos and lead testing/abatement
SB 721 balcony inspections apply to 3+ unit buildings with elevated elements

answers.summary: The best paybacks come from interior upgrades on 1960s-80s units (new LVP flooring, kitchen and bath refresh, lighting), adding in-unit washer/dryers where plumbing allows, and RUBS. Typical spend is $20,000-$40,000 per unit for a $250-$450 monthly premium, or about 10-15% return on cost. Market evidence caps the upside at about the $500 gap between 1970s and 2010s rents.
answers.answer:
### The ceiling
CBRE's Q2 2026 vintage data shows **$2,460 (1970s) vs. $2,955 (2010s)**, a gap of about $495 per month. A renovated older unit rarely closes all of it, because location, parking, amenities and A/C still separate classes. Aim to capture **50-80%** of the gap.

### Renovation menu (practitioner ranges, 2026)
| Item | Cost per unit | Typical rent premium | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classic interior package (LVP, paint, lighting, hardware, blinds) | $6,000-$12,000 | $100-$200/mo | Fastest payback |
| Full kitchen (shaker cabinets, quartz, SS appliances) | $12,000-$20,000 | $150-$250/mo | Bundle with flooring |
| Bath refresh (vanity, tile surround, fixtures) | $5,000-$10,000 | $50-$100/mo | |
| In-unit washer/dryer (stackable) | $3,000-$6,000 if plumbing and venting are feasible | $50-$100/mo | Big draw in Oxnard and Ventura |
| Mini-split A/C | $4,000-$7,000 | $50-$125/mo | Pays in inland submarkets (Simi, Moorpark, Thousand Oaks, Santa Paula) |
| RUBS / water submeters | $0-$1,500 | $75-$150/mo recovery | See Q50 |
| ADU or garage conversion on 2-4 unit lots | $150,000-$300,000 per ADU | Full 1BR/studio rent | State ADU law streamlines permits |
| Covered parking, storage, EV charging | Varies | $25-$75/mo | |

**All-in example:** A $30,000 interior plus washer/dryer earning $350/month ($4,200/yr) is about a **14% return on cost**. At a 5% cap rate that creates about $84,000 of value, or roughly 2.8x the spend.

### What to watch
- **AB 1482 just cause:** You can renovate only at natural turnover. A "substantial remodel" termination requires permits, at least 30 days of required vacancy and relocation money. Don't plan renovations on forced turnover.
- **Coastal Zone:** Exterior or parking changes near the beach (Ventura Pierpont, Oxnard Shores, Port Hueneme) may need coastal permits.
- **Permits and code:** Unpermitted prior work surfaces in plan check (Q58).

answers.summary: Inland, A/C is close to a must-have. On the coast it's a modest plus. In-unit laundry commands about $50-$100 a month, and covered or assigned parking matters most in dense Oxnard, Port Hueneme and Midtown Ventura neighborhoods, where on-street parking is saturated by overcrowded households.
answers.answer:
### Air conditioning
- **Coastal (Ventura west of Victoria/Mills, Oxnard, Port Hueneme, Pierpont):** The marine layer keeps summers mild. Many 1960s-80s buildings have no A/C, and tenants accept wall heaters and fans. Adding a mini-split brings about **$25-$75 a month**, more during recent heat waves.
- **Inland (Simi Valley, Moorpark, Thousand Oaks/Newbury Park, Camarillo east of Lewis Rd, Santa Paula, Fillmore, Ojai):** Summer highs regularly top 90-100°F. Units without A/C lease slower and at a **$75-$150 discount**, or turn over faster.

### In-unit laundry
- New Class A all has in-unit washer/dryers. In older buildings, laundry is usually a shared coin or card room, often contracted to a vendor that splits revenue.
- Practitioner premium for in-unit washer/dryer: **$50-$100 a month**. Hookups only: about $25-$50.
- Shared laundry income typically runs about $10-$25 per unit per month. Count that loss if you convert to in-unit.

### Parking
- Most 1960s-80s garden buildings have **about 1 space per unit** in tuck-under carports. 2BR and 3BR households in Oxnard and Port Hueneme often have 2-3 cars (see overcrowding, Q58).
- Assigned or covered parking in tight neighborhoods (South Oxnard, La Colonia, Midtown and Westside Ventura, Port Hueneme near NBVC) supports about a **$25-$75 premium**, and garages can rent for $100-$200 or more.
- State law **AB 2097** (2023) removed minimum parking requirements near major transit, and ADU law limits replacement-parking requirements. That helps add units, but crowded parking can hurt resident satisfaction.

### Underwriting
Compare comps on the same amenity basis. A 2BR with A/C, in-unit laundry and two covered spaces in Simi Valley can lease $200-$300 above an otherwise similar unit without them. On the coast the spread is closer to $100-$150.

answers.summary: Housing Choice Vouchers are a meaningful but minority share of the market. Payment standards are now set by ZIP code (Small Area FMRs) and are competitive with market rents: in Ventura they run about $2,746-$2,832 for a 2BR including utilities. Source-of-income discrimination is illegal in California, so voucher holders must be screened like any other applicant.
answers.answer:
### Who administers vouchers
- **Ventura Housing (Housing Authority of the City of San Buenaventura):** City of Ventura. HCV office at 11122 Snapdragon St.
- **Area Housing Authority of the County of Ventura:** Camarillo, Moorpark, Ojai, Simi Valley, Thousand Oaks, Fillmore and unincorporated areas.
- **Oxnard Housing Authority** (Oxnard), plus the **Santa Paula** and **Port Hueneme** housing authorities.

### Payment standards (Ventura Housing, effective Oct 1, 2025)
Since January 2025 the Oxnard-Thousand Oaks-Ventura metro has been one of HUD's required **Small Area FMR** areas, so payment standards vary by ZIP code.

| ZIP | Efficiency | 1BR | 2BR | 3BR | 4BR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 93001 (Downtown/Westside/Pierpont) | $1,960 | $2,321 | $2,746 | $3,652 | $4,264 |
| 93003 (Midtown/East) | $1,970 | $2,374 | $2,814 | $3,666 | $4,283 |
| 93004 (East End/Saticoy) | $2,033 | $2,410 | $2,832 | $3,724 | $4,325 |
| Metro FMR FY2026 (project-based) | $1,998 | $2,250 | $2,693 | $3,652 | $4,240 |

These are gross figures. The contract rent plus the tenant utility allowance (Q49) must fit under the standard, and the rent must pass a **rent reasonableness** test against comparable unassisted units. At move-in, the tenant pays no more than **40% of adjusted income**.

### How prevalent
In practice, vouchers cluster in older Class C buildings in Oxnard, Ventura (Midtown/Westside), Santa Paula and Simi Valley, plus project-based units in affordable communities. In a typical older 20-50 unit building, expect anywhere from 0% to 15-20% voucher tenants.

### Owner considerations
- **Pros:** reliable HAP payments, longer tenancies, and payment standards near or above Class C market rent (a 93003 2BR at $2,814 gross is about $2,660 net of a $150 utility allowance, at or above many 1970s rents).
- **Cons:** HQS/NSPIRE-standard inspections, 60-day notice for rent-increase requests, possible funding-related limits on increases, and paperwork.
- **Law:** SB 329 (2020) makes refusing voucher holders source-of-income discrimination. Apply the same screening criteria to everyone, and don't apply minimum-income tests to the voucher-paid portion of the rent.

answers.summary: Overcrowding is among the highest in California in parts of the county: about 26% of Oxnard renter households (11% severely) vs. about 13-15% countywide. Unpermitted units (garage conversions, extra bedrooms) are common in older 2-4 unit and small walk-up buildings. Buyers value only legal units and treat bootleg income as upside or as a risk to cure.

Drivers: farmworker and extended-family households, and high rents relative to agricultural and service wages (see Q17).

### Unpermitted units
- **Where:** pre-1980 duplexes to fourplexes and small walk-ups in Oxnard (La Colonia, South Oxnard), Santa Paula, Fillmore, Port Hueneme and Ventura Westside and Midtown. Typical forms are garage conversions, "bonus" rooms, studios carved from laundry or storage rooms, and units added to commercial or mixed-use lots.
- **How to detect:** compare the rent roll to the **Assessor's unit count** and permit history, check meters and utility accounts, and walk every unit, including garages.

### How buyers underwrite it
1. **Value on legal units only.** Treat income from unpermitted units as upside, often valued at a higher cap rate or excluded.
2. **Legalization path:** State ADU law makes many conversions permittable. AB 2533 (2024) limits a city's ability to deny permits for unpermitted ADUs built before 2020 except for health and safety reasons. Budget $25,000-$75,000+ per unit for plans, fees and upgrades (fire separation, egress, electrical).
3. **Risk if not curable:** Removing an occupied illegal unit can trigger relocation obligations under AB 1482 just-cause rules, and code enforcement can red-tag the unit.
4. **Lenders** usually size loans to legal units only and may require a zoning report.

**So what:** In Oxnard and Santa Paula especially, a "6-unit" listing may be 4 legal units. Price it that way, and treat legalization as your value-add.
